kid.question: What troubles does God promise to remove from His flock?

options.text: Hunger and fear of attack
Cold and fear of storms
Thirst and fear of darkness
Illness and fear of travel

kid.explanation: The flock will no longer be prey or be consumed by hunger, and no one will make them afraid.

kid.question: Who are the sheep in God's pasture?

options.text: The people of Babylon
The people of Israel
The people of Egypt
The people of Moab

kid.explanation: God identifies the flock as people and names the house of Israel as His people.

kid.question: What is Ezekiel told to address at the beginning of chapter 36?

options.text: The mountains of Israel
The islands of the sea
The borders of neighboring nations
The roads of returning exiles

kid.explanation: Ezekiel is told to prophesy to Israel's mountains; the address includes hills, rivers, valleys, wastes, and cities.

kid.question: What do the enemies say about Israel's old high places?

options.text: They now belong to us
They will be shared with Judah
They must be given to Egypt
They cannot be lived in again

kid.explanation: The enemy boasts that the ancient high places are now theirs to possess.

kid.question: What will happen on Israel's mountains when the people return?

options.text: Camps will spread and weapons be stored
Branches will grow and fields be planted
Fortresses will rise and soldiers be trained
Silver will be mined and coins be made

kid.explanation: The mountains will yield fruit for returning Israel, and God promises the land will be tilled and sown.

kid.question: What does God promise for the ruined cities?

options.text: Kings will sell them to foreigners
Soldiers will turn them into camps
People will live in them again
Farmers will leave them for villages

kid.explanation: God will multiply the people, inhabit the cities, and rebuild the wastes.

kid.question: Why were the people scattered among other countries?

options.text: They tried to rebuild their walls without permission
They refused to give their land to strangers
They failed to join their king in battle
They polluted their land with bloodshed and idols

kid.explanation: God says their bloodshed, idols, and conduct defiled the land, and He scattered and judged them accordingly.

kid.question: Where does God promise to bring the scattered people?

options.text: Into a larger foreign empire
Into the mountains of Egypt
Back into their own land
Across the sea to new islands

kid.explanation: God promises to gather them from all countries and bring them into their own land.

kid.question: What action pictures God's promise in Ezekiel 36:25?

options.text: Anointing their heads with fresh oil
Sprinkling clean water upon them
Passing them through a refining fire
Dressing them in newly washed robes

kid.explanation: God promises to sprinkle clean water and cleanse them from their filthiness and idols.

kid.question: What does God promise to put within His people?

options.text: A new name
A new language
A new song
A new spirit

kid.explanation: God promises a new heart and spirit, then says His spirit will help them walk in His statutes and keep His judgments.

high-school.question: What do the promises of safety and provision help Israel recognize?

options.text: Their former shepherds have earned renewed authority over them
The Lord is with them and they are His people
Their enemies have become the lawful owners of their pasture
The surrounding nations have taken over the Lord's covenant with them

high-school.explanation: The closing verses explicitly link the restored flock's experience with knowing the Lord is with them and they are His people.

high-school.question: Why does God address the land's humiliation before announcing restoration?

options.text: The neighboring nations have offered to rebuild the land's ruined sanctuaries
Enemy claims and mockery have treated His land as their possession
A successful harvest has caused disputes about dividing the land's income
Israel's returning rulers have asked permission to enlarge the land's borders

high-school.explanation: God names hostile possession, prey, infamy, and shame, then announces that the surrounding nations will bear shame.

high-school.question: How does the land's renewal serve the returning people?

options.text: Fruitful mountains and rebuilt settlements provide a place for them to live
Fruitful mountains provide tribute so that they can remain in foreign countries
Rebuilt settlements provide bases so that they can conquer neighboring nations
Rebuilt settlements provide markets so that they can sell their inheritance abroad

high-school.explanation: Fruit is for returning Israel; tilled land, inhabited cities, increased people and animals, and renewed inheritance support settlement.

high-school.question: How does God answer the saying quoted in Ezekiel 36:13?

options.text: God confirms that the land belongs to the strongest army
God orders the people to move permanently to foreign fields
God requires neighboring nations to replace each former inhabitant
God promises an end to its bereavement and reproach

high-school.explanation: The promise directly counters the charge that the land devours people: it will no longer bereave its nations or bear their reproach.

high-school.question: What is the relation between Israel's conduct and exile?

options.text: Exile is presented as punishment for their ancestors' forgotten vows
Exile is presented as preparation to govern the surrounding nations
Exile is presented as God's judgment in response to their own deeds
Exile is presented as refuge from a land unable to support them

high-school.explanation: God names defilement, bloodshed, and idols, and says He judged and scattered them according to their ways and doings.

high-school.question: Why does the condition of the exiles concern God's name?

options.text: They have persuaded the nations to stop using any names for their rulers
They are identified as His people while displaced from His land
They are appointed to teach His name after returning to their original cities
They are required to replace His name with the names of foreign gods

high-school.explanation: The nations identify them as the Lord's people who have gone out of His land; God calls His name profaned and promises to sanctify it.

high-school.question: What reason does God give in Ezekiel 36:22 for acting?

options.text: He acts for His holy name's sake before the nations
Reward for Israel's faithful conduct during the exile
Approval of the nations' repentance after their earlier conquests
Payment for the returning captives' service to their foreign rulers

high-school.explanation: God says He acts for His holy name's sake, not for Israel's sakes, and the nations will know He is the Lord.

high-school.question: How does the restoration promise go beyond geography?

options.text: Return to the land is delayed until every ruined city is rebuilt
Return to the land is exchanged for influence at a foreign court
Return to the land is divided into rival priestly and royal territories
Return to the land is joined to cleansing and inward renewal

high-school.explanation: The promise moves from gathering and bringing home to clean water, a new heart, and a new spirit.

high-school.question: Which contrast expresses the promised inward change?

options.text: An empty heart is filled with the memories of conquest
A fearful heart is strengthened by a heart of bronze
A stony heart is replaced by a heart of flesh
A divided heart is balanced by the advice of two kings

high-school.explanation: God promises to remove the stony heart and give a heart of flesh, along with a new spirit.

high-school.question: What is the intended effect of God's spirit within the people?

options.text: They walk in His statutes and carry out His judgments
They return to temple service as rulers over foreign nations
They receive permission to establish a different set of laws
They inherit the offices held by the exiles' former captors

high-school.explanation: God links putting His spirit within them directly to walking in His statutes and keeping and doing His judgments.

expert.question: What does the oracle's closing identification clarify about the shepherd metaphor?

options.text: The pasture denotes a new temple in which animals replace the restored people
The pasture denotes a foreign kingdom whose rulers become Israel's new shepherds
The flock consists of foreign rulers appointed to govern the people of Israel
The flock consists of human covenant people with the Lord as their God

expert.explanation: The text explicitly calls the flock men and identifies Israel as God's people and Him as their God.

expert.question: How are the land's features related to hostile possession in Ezekiel 36:1-7?

options.text: Mountains, waterways, wastes, and cities share the shame of hostile appropriation
Mountains receive comfort while the occupied cities are excluded from the address
Rivers and valleys accuse mountains of refusing refuge to the displaced people
Wastes receive judgment while the cities negotiate an alliance with foreign rulers

expert.explanation: The address expands across the land's features and settlements, naming their exposure to possession, prey, derision, and shame.

expert.question: What reversal links the neighboring nations with the mountains of Israel?

options.text: The nations will bear shame while the mountains yield fruit for returning Israel
The nations will abandon agriculture while Israel buys food from their remaining cities
The nations will inherit the mountains while returning Israel bears the shame of exile
The nations will cultivate the mountains while Israel remains permanently among them

expert.explanation: After promising shame for the surrounding nations, God promises fruitful branches for His people, who are at hand to come.

expert.question: What makes restoration more than a return to the land's former population?

options.text: It includes ending settled agriculture in favor of a return to nomadic movement
It includes transferring the land's fruitfulness to nations that had remained neutral
It includes increased people and beasts and doing better than at the beginnings
It includes replacing ancestral holdings with a permanent royal ownership system

expert.explanation: God promises multiplication, renewed settlement and inheritance, and to do better than at their beginnings.

expert.question: How does the account distinguish the cause of dispersion from a further concern in exile?

options.text: A royal dispute brings migration; leadership among nations becomes associated with replacing God's covenant
Ancestral disobedience brings famine; rebuilding among nations becomes associated with restoring God's temple
Foreign invasion brings reward; settlement among nations becomes associated with teaching God's law
Corrupt deeds bring judgment; dispersion among nations becomes associated with profaning God's name

expert.explanation: Their deeds defile the land and lead to scattering; among the nations His name is profaned through their identified displacement.

expert.question: What distinction governs the declared rationale for intervention?

options.text: Israel's military strength grounds action rather than the need to cleanse its idols
The nations' repentance grounds action rather than Israel's return from exile
God's holy name grounds action rather than Israel's deserving conduct
Israel's greater population grounds action rather than God's concern for His name

expert.explanation: God explicitly says the action is not for their sakes but for His name, which was profaned among the nations.

expert.question: How is recognition by the nations related to the gathering promise?

options.text: They will know the Lord through private instruction replacing public restoration
They will know the Lord as He is sanctified in Israel before their eyes
They will know the Lord when Israel abandons its claim to return to its land
They will know the Lord after Israel joins their armies against its former rulers

expert.explanation: God says the nations will know He is the Lord when sanctified in Israel before them, followed by the gathering from countries.

expert.question: Which sequence follows the promise's movement from external location to conduct?

options.text: Cleansing, replacing the priesthood, new sacrifices, joining the neighboring armies
Gathering home, cleansing, new heart and spirit, walking in God's statutes
Gathering home, installing a foreign ruler, new taxes, rebuilding royal defenses
Cleansing, dividing the nation, returning to exile, walking under foreign laws

expert.explanation: The promise moves through gathering and return, cleansing, inward replacement, and Spirit-enabled obedience.

expert.question: How are the cleansing and heart images related in Ezekiel 36:25-26?

options.text: Removal of defilement is joined to replacement of an unresponsive inward condition
Cleansing concerns polluted fields while heart replacement concerns the city's new ruler
Cleansing concerns foreign peoples while heart replacement concerns Israel's returning captives
Removal of bodily illness is joined to restoration of the people's physical strength

expert.explanation: Water cleanses from filthiness and idols, while the removal of the stony heart and gift of a fleshly heart portray inward renewal.

expert.question: What prevents reading the new spirit as merely a change of feeling?

options.text: Its presence is connected with recovering sanctuary songs for the people's communal mourning
Its presence is expressly connected with keeping and doing God's judgments
Its presence is connected with gaining the ability to interpret prophetic dreams
Its presence is connected with teaching the law to nations gathered at Jerusalem

expert.explanation: The gift of a new spirit is followed by God's own spirit causing them to walk in His statutes and do His judgments.
